activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, usually on April 4 or 5, families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings.
story:
Zack found the box on the top shelf of his grandfather's closet, which smelled like pencil shavings and cough drops. Inside was a coin, a receipt from 1987, and a note in shaky handwriting that said "not a counterfeit, whatever your uncle says." Zack turned the coin under his desk lamp. It was heavy for its size, and when he tapped it with a spoon it rang instead of clunked, the way real metal did. His grandfather had told him once that a good coin was an alloy, silver mixed with a little copper, and that pure anything was too soft to last. Zack had no idea what the note meant, but it was clearly something his grandfather had wanted someone to find.

At dinner, his mom said the family would go to the cemetery on April fifth. "Qingming," she said. "Your grandfather's family always did it. We visit the graves, clean them, and leave offerings." Zack put down his fork. He had never heard of it, even though his grandfather had lived with them for three years before he died. Had he just not been paying attention? He thought about all the Aprils that had gone by, and about how many things his grandfather had done quietly, without announcing them, like the way he called the lawnmower "hibernating" every winter instead of saying it was broken.

Zack asked his friend Forest and his classmate Ira to come along, mostly because he did not want to stand at a grave with only his mom and his uncle arguing about the coin. Ira, whose family did Qingming every year, brought a small broom and a bag of oranges. "You sweep the stone first," Ira said, demonstrating with quick, tidy strokes, like the gravestone was a countertop. "Then you leave the offerings. My grandma says the food isn't really for eating. But she always brings Grandpa's favorite cookies anyway, so I'm not sure she believes herself."

Zack swept his grandfather's stone while his uncle told a story about a fishing trip that ended with a drowned cooler and a very angry goose. Forest laughed so hard he dropped an orange, and it rolled down the little slope and stopped against a fence post, as if it had chosen its spot. Zack set the coin on the flat top of the stone, next to the oranges. Maybe nothing happened after you died, and maybe something did; he couldn't see either way, any more than you could see what made the coin ring. But he noticed his mom stopped crying, or at least stopped wiping her eyes, and started telling a goose story of her own.

On the walk back, Mr. Wiśniewski from next door was out in his garden, and he waved them over to look at his tomato seedlings. Zack's uncle handed him an orange. "From Grandpa," Zack said.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In Richard Connell's 1924 story The Most Dangerous Game, the island's name, Ship-Trap Island, and sailors' fear of it hint at the danger waiting there.
story:
Amelia slid The Most Dangerous Game across the library table and dropped into the chair beside Matias. "Ms. Nakamura wants us to find foreshadowing and symbolism by Thursday, and explain what they suggest," she said. "I've read this thing twice and I still feel like I'm guessing."

Matias spun the paperback to face himself and flipped to the first page. Louis-Thomas leaned over from the other side, chewing the end of a pencil. "It's just an island," he said. "A guy falls off a yacht. Where's the clue?"

Amelia inhaled the smell of old paper and tried again, slower this time. "Everything in a story is chosen," she said, more to herself than to them. "So why this island, with this name?" She ran her finger down the opening page and stopped. "There. The sailors call it Ship-Trap Island. And they're scared of it. Both of those things happen before anything dangerous does."

Matias sat back. "So the name is doing something."

"Test it," Amelia said. She grabbed a sticky note and wrote the island's name on it, then wrote fear beside it. "If a place is called Ship-Trap Island and even sailors who've never landed there are afraid of it, what does that suggest about what's waiting on it?" She looked at Louis-Thomas. "You're Rainsford. You wash up on the shore. What do you expect?"

"Trouble," Louis-Thomas said. "Big trouble." He wrote it down, then added, "So that's foreshadowing because it hints ahead. And the island could be a symbol, too, because a trap isn't only a place."

Matias grinned and pointed his pencil at her. "You just did the assignment. 'Suggest.' That's the word Ms. Nakamura kept using."

Amelia felt something buoyant lift in her chest, though she made herself stay careful. "One clue isn't a pattern yet," she said. She paged forward, hunting for other signs, and when Ms. Nakamura passed their table on her way to the reference desk, Amelia raised her hand. "Can we present on how a place name can warn the reader before the characters figure it out?"

Ms. Nakamura paused. "Bring me your evidence on Thursday," she said, and moved on.

"Thursday," Matias repeated in a low voice. "That's two days to find three more examples."

Amelia turned to a clean page and wrote their first one at the top. She would worry like a diplomat negotiating a truce, calmly and on both sides of the question, but the search had already begun.

"Next story," she said, and pulled the anthology toward her.

"Pick a scary one," said Louis-Thomas.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Health agencies recommend scrubbing hands with soap for at least 20 seconds, including after changing a diaper and before preparing food.
story:
Elizabeth stood in Ms. Augustin's backyard with eighteen-month-old Theo on her hip, watching him grab at the wind chime by the patio door. Ms. Augustin had left a list on the fridge, a phone number, and a jar of pureed pears, and had said, "He'll be easy, I promise," in the voice of someone who wanted to believe it. Elizabeth had said yes mostly for the ten dollars, and now that the gate had clicked shut behind Ms. Augustin, the backyard felt very large and very quiet.

The trouble started at the sandbox. Theo dug with a plastic shovel, triumphant, until a smell drifted up that made Elizabeth's nose wrinkle. She checked his diaper and wished she hadn't looked. The change itself went badly at first, with Theo rolling onto his side mid-wipe, one sock defiantly kicked off into the grass, but she got the new diaper on and the old one sealed in a plastic bag, and she carried both of them inside feeling like she had won something.

At the kitchen sink she turned on the water and soaped her hands, then wondered how long was long enough. She remembered the poster in the school nurse's office: twenty seconds of scrubbing, at least. She didn't have a timer, but she did have a song from third-grade music class, and she was pretty sure that one run-through took about ten seconds. So she hummed it once, all the way to the end, then hummed it again while she scrubbed between her fingers and around her thumbs. When the last note faded, she rinsed and dried her hands on the towel shaped like a duck.

"Okay," she told Theo, who was standing at her knee with pears on his mind. "Lunch." She spooned the puree into a bowl, and only then did she stop with the spoon in the air. If the poster said twenty seconds, and it did, she had a suspicion it wasn't random advice. It was probably meant for exactly this: after changing a diaper, before handling food. She had guessed right without knowing why the guess mattered, and the thought made her stand a little straighter, like a jury that had reached the right verdict.

Theo ate the pears with both hands and deposited a portion in his hair. Elizabeth wiped him down, wiped the tray, and carried him back outside, where the afternoon had gone gold on the fence boards. She sat him in the grass and texted her mother a question about whether mashed banana could be preserved in the fridge for the next day, then looked up at the sound of the gate latch.

"Verdict?" Ms. Augustin called, stepping onto the patio. "Did we survive?"

"He's fine," Elizabeth said, "but next time you owe me two songs' worth of hazard pay."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was started in 1967 by John van Hengel.
story:
Harper signed in at the library basement door at nine fifty-eight, two minutes before the food bank opened, and Mr. He handed her a hairnet and a box of dented cans. "Sort those by type," he said. "Pasta with pasta, beans with beans. The truck comes at noon."

Beside her, Lou was already sorting, fast and sideways-glancing, like the cans might escape. "I want the front table," Lou whispered. "My mom's coming at noon, and she's never seen me do anything useful." Lou's mother had been laid off in March, and Lou had been quieter at school ever since.

Harper opened a can of green beans, checked the lid, and set it in the beans section. But halfway through the box she noticed something odd: the canned-goods shelf was almost empty, while the pasta shelf was saturated, rows and rows of elbows and spaghetti stacked to the edge. She counted. Fifty-three pasta, eleven cans. That didn't make sense unless people were choosing cans first, which meant by noon there would be nothing left on that shelf and a line of neighbors waiting.

"I'm going to move some pasta to the storeroom," she told Lou, "and put cans where families can reach them. If people take cans first, we need cans up front." Lou hesitated, then grabbed an armful. Together they rebuilt the shelf, cans at eye level, pasta behind.

At eleven thirty, Mr. He came through and frowned at the wall of the break room, where a yellowed poster hung. Harper had read it on her break: the first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was started in 1967 by John van Hengel. "Where did all the pasta go?" Mr. He asked.

"I hid it," Harper said. "People take the cans first. Watch." She pointed at the line already forming by the doors, a grandmother with two kids, a man carrying his own empty grocery sack. Sure enough, the cans began moving, one by one, and the pasta held.

Mr. He watched for a full minute, then nodded once, like a rudder settling a boat back on course. "Good eye," he said. "Lou, you're on the front table today."

At noon the truck arrived, and Lou's mother came in right behind it. Lou stood behind the table, handing a bag of beans to the grandmother, her back straight, her smile so wide it looked like it might fall off.

"That one's mine," Lou said, pointing at her mother in the doorway, and waved with both hands.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: The 'butterflies' people feel when nervous come from adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach toward the muscles.
story:
At noon Tyler sat in the corner booth of the coffee shop with a turkey sandwich he could not finish. He had eaten exactly one half, and even that felt like a mistake. His date with Destiny was at seven, and his stomach had been doing something strange all day, a light, fluttery feeling, like something small was loose in there. He wondered if he was coming down with a bug, except he felt fine otherwise, and his heart kept thumping fast even though he was just sitting there.

He pushed the plate away and tried to quantify the problem, because numbers always made him feel better. Half a sandwich in four hours. Heart rate up maybe twenty beats from his normal resting pace. Stomach flutter level, if he had to give it a score, a seven out of ten. Whatever this was, it had started the moment he'd texted Destiny to confirm the movie, and it had not stopped since.

The door chimed and Savanna came in, uniform still on from her shift behind the counter. She slid into the booth across from him and looked at his abandoned lunch. "You look like my brother before his driving test," she said. "You're nervous."

"Is that what this is?" Tyler asked. "It feels like my stomach is the problem, not my brain."

Savanna shrugged. "My mom calls them butterflies. She says her mom had them too, so I guess it's hereditary." She stole a pickle off his plate. "You should probably look it up instead of sitting here imagining you have some rare disease."

He did look it up, right there at the table, phone balanced beside the mustard. The answer made him sit up straight. The butterflies people feel when nervous come from adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach toward the muscles. He read it twice. His heart was racing and his stomach felt fluttery because they were connected, not because he was sick, and the whole thing was his body getting ready like something big was about to happen. He supposed a first date was something big.

"So it's not a disease," he told Savanna, "it's just adrenaline." He tested the idea the only way he could, by taking the last bite of the sandwich, chewing slowly, and paying attention. The flutter was still there, but it felt different now that he knew its name, more like an engine warming up than a warning.

Savanna clocked back in behind the counter, and Tyler walked to the theater early so his legs could use some of that blood. When Destiny came jogging up the sidewalk in her yellow jacket, his heart gave one hard thump, and this time he noticed it the way you notice a friend waving from across a street. He held the door open and asked, "Butterflies?" and she laughed and said, "Terrible ones," and he grinned because now he knew exactly what she meant.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda.
story:
Sara had one hour before the library closed, and she still needed a topic for Ms. Tse's research project. She wandered past the new books shelf, where a poster advertised the summer reading club: "Everyone is joining! Don't be the only one left out!" Below it, a photo of a famous singer grinned over the words "Even she reads here." Sara stopped. Something about the poster itched at her, the way a sock seam does when you can't take your shoe off.

She found River at a table near the windows, arranging old wartime posters Ms. Tse had brought in from the archives. One showed a soldier pointing straight out: "Everyone is buying bonds. Are YOU?" Another showed a grim-faced factory worker under the words "SLOTH kills our boys." A third had a movie star in a nurse's cap holding a tin can.

"These are supposed to be about the war," River said. "But half of them are about me somehow."

"That's the point," Sara said slowly. She tapped the pointing soldier. "It makes you feel like the whole world already agreed, and you're the last holdout. Like that reading club poster." She spun the newspaper microfilm reel Ms. Tse had suggested, hunting for something about how posters were made. An article from the late 1930s mentioned a group that had been founded to teach regular people to spot exactly these tricks. She read the name twice to be sure. "The Institute for Propaganda Analysis," she said out loud. "Nineteen thirty-seven. In the United States."

River leaned over. "So people back then were already tired of being pushed around by posters?"

"Regular people," Sara said. "Not soldiers, not politicians. Just people." Her mind was moving now, the way it did when a puzzle piece finally shows its edge. She had a theory: the wartime posters and the reading club poster worked the same way, and she could test it. She flipped her notebook to a fresh page and made three columns. "Everybody's doing it," she wrote at the top of the first. "Words that make you feel something before you can think," went over the second. "Famous face," over the third.

Then they went hunting. The soldier poster fit column one. "SLOTH kills our boys" fit column two, since sloth made it sound like resting on a Sunday was practically a crime against the nation, which even River agreed was a stretch. The movie star fit column three. So did the singer. By the time Saoirse wandered over from the biography section, the page was full, and vapor from River's breath had fogged the cold window beside them in little clouds that shrank and grew.

"Looks contagious," Saoirse said, nodding at the page. "Like everyone's catching posters."

"It kind of is," Sara said. "That's how they spread. The good news is you can wash your hands." Ms. Tse stopped at their table on her rounds, glanced at the three columns, and raised one eyebrow. Sara slid the notebook toward her. "I think I have my topic," she said. "Unless everyone else already picked it."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: The placebo effect is when people feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, simply because they expect it to help.
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:42 p.m., which was late for Malachi, who usually saved his best theories for the walk to school. "That drink WORKS," he posted. "Two bottles of VoltCharge and I dropped fifteen seconds off my mile. My legs felt like they had opinions and all of them were fast."

Hailey was doing homework at the kitchen table, but she put her pencil down. Fifteen seconds was a lot. She typed back, "Fifteen seconds is huge. What was your time before?" He sent a screenshot of his running app, then three flexing emojis, then a photo of the bottle with lightning bolts on it, in case anyone doubted its seriousness.

Dalia joined in. "My brother drinks those and says the same thing. I think they taste like flat soda that went to a party." The chat debated this for a while. Hailey read the label photo closely. Caffeine, sure, but Malachi drank it at six in the evening and slept fine, which didn't fit. Then she found something on her laptop and scrolled until the kitchen went quiet around her. She typed, "There's a thing called the placebo effect. It's when people feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, like a sugar pill, just because they expect it to help." Malachi replied with a single question mark. She added, "Meet me at the track Saturday. Bring your fast legs."

Saturday, she brought two bottles in her gym bag, both wrapped in plain white tape with A and B written in marker. Bottle A was VoltCharge, poured in at home. Bottle B was the same color of juice, basically sugar water, nothing in it that did anything. She didn't tell Malachi which was which. He drank A before his first mile, and ran it in 7:02. He drank B, wiped his mouth, said "that stuff is strong," and ran the second in 6:58.

"Same brand both times," he announced, hands on his knees.

"Sure," Hailey said.

Dalia, holding the stopwatch, looked at Hailey over Malachi's head. Hailey looked back and peeled a corner of tape off bottle B, very slowly, like a game show reveal. Malachi read the label underneath twice.

"Okay," he said. "So how fast can I run if I believe in juice?"

Dalia started laughing so hard she nearly dropped the watch, and Hailey said, "That's actually the experiment now," and got out her phone to message the coach.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A prime checker must handle numbers below 2 separately, because 0, 1 and negative numbers are not prime, yet a divisor loop starting at 2 finds nothing to reject them.
story:
Lucy sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her laptop balanced on a stack of pillows, because the desk chair made her shoulders ache after an hour of typing. On the screen was half a program.

She was writing it for a small contest Ms. Sow had mentioned after class: a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime. Lucy had typed the loop already, the part that tried dividing the number by everything starting at 2. If no divisor worked, it printed "prime." It felt finished, except that it didn't run yet, and she wanted to test it before her friend Corinne came over to study.

Corinne arrived at four with her math workbook under one arm and two granola bars, one of which she set beside Lucy's laptop without comment. "Is that the prime thing?" she asked, dropping onto the bed. "Mine keeps breaking."

"Mine's not even running," Lucy said. She fixed a missing colon, ran it, and typed 7. Prime. She typed 9. Not prime. She typed 13, then 15, and the answers came back correct each time. She was starting to feel smug when Corinne leaned over and said, "Try zero."

Lucy typed 0 and pressed enter. The program thought for less than a blink and printed "prime." She stared at it. "That's wrong," she said. "Zero is definitely not prime. Everyone knows that."

"Then why did it say it was?"

Lucy read her own loop out loud, tracing it with a finger on the screen. The loop tried divisors starting at 2. For zero, she realized, it never found any divisor to reject the number, so it fell straight through to the "prime" answer. "It's not checking anything below 2," she said slowly. "Zero, one, negative numbers. The loop starts at 2, so it just skips them and calls them all prime." She grabbed a scrap of paper and wrote: 0, 1, negatives, handle before loop.

"So you check those first?" Corinne asked.

"Before the loop even starts." Lucy added three lines at the top, so that anything less than 2 got an immediate "not prime." Then she tested it, and in a vain attempt to break it again, Corinne typed negative numbers, 1, 0, and a number so long it ran off the screen. The program answered every one correctly.

Lucy saved the file twice, once to the desktop and once to a flash drive, because Ms. Sow collected the entries on Friday. Then she peeled the granola bar open and handed the wrapper to Corinne to throw away. "Your turn," she said. "Type something. Anything. I want to watch it persist through the worst number you've got."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Using separate cutting boards for raw meat and for ready-to-eat foods like salad prevents cross-contamination, the spread of bacteria from one food to another.
story:
Aiden stood in the produce aisle with his mom's list in his hand, trying to allocate the last of the money she had given him. Chicken thighs, a bag of salad, bread, and one lemon took most of the twenty dollars, so he put back the expensive strawberries and chose the smaller box. His mom was working the late shift, and tonight the dinner job was his.

He was reaching for a head of lettuce when he heard someone say his name. Lena from science class was three feet away, holding a jar of pasta sauce. "You cook?" she asked, looking at his basket.

"Dinner tonight. My mom's working." He lifted the chicken package so she could see it. "Chicken and salad."

"Oh, we did a unit on that," Lena said. "Raw meat and stuff. Mr. Tse made us watch a video."

At home, Aiden laid everything out on the counter. The rain had started on the walk from the store, and by the time he got inside, his hood was dark with precipitation and his shoes squeaked on the kitchen floor. He turned the oven on, unwrapped the chicken, and cut the thighs into strips on the big wooden cutting board, the one with the intricate pattern of burned lines around its edge that his grandpa had made years ago.

He washed his hands, then set the board by the sink. Next came the salad. He pulled the lettuce apart, rinsed it, and was about to lay it on the board when he stopped. The board still smelled faintly of chicken. He thought about the video Lena had mentioned, and about what his mom had said once, that raw chicken could leave things behind even when a surface looked clean. The bacteria, whatever they were, had moved from the meat to the wood, and if he chopped lettuce on top, they would move again from the wood into food nobody would cook. It was a chain he couldn't see, but he could break it.

He took the small green plastic board from the cupboard instead, the one his mom used only for fruit, and set the lettuce on that. Then he scrubbed the wooden board with hot soapy water until his hands were pink.

When his little brother wandered in, hungry and whiny, Aiden gave him a bowl of rinsed grapes first so he wouldn't hover over the stove. He cooked the chicken until the juices ran clear, tossed the salad with lemon and a little salt, and had everything on plates by the time headlights swept the window.

His mom came in shaking rain off her jacket. She looked at the two boards stacked by the sink, one scrubbed and one still damp, then at Aiden.

"You used the green one for the salad?"

"Yeah," Aiden said. "The wooden one had raw chicken on it."

She set down her keys and hugged him, still cold from the rain. "Smart," she said, picking up her fork.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The First Amendment to the US Constitution protects freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly and petitioning the government.
story:
Ivy spread the photocopied page across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with a fork, a salt shaker, and her mother's mug of cold coffee. Mr. Reddy had assigned each student one amendment from the Bill of Rights and told them to explain it, in their own words, to somebody at home. Ivy had drawn the First. She had been staring at it for twenty minutes, which felt like a personal insult, because the First was supposed to be the easy one.

She called Lilou, who was drawing the Third and claimed her only task was to explain that soldiers could not be parked in your spare bedroom. "That's a whole amendment?" Ivy said. "Mine has five things crammed into it. Religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. Petitioning. Do you know what petitioning is?" Lilou did not, and suggested Ivy look it up before Monday, then hung up to invest her remaining energy in a poster of a soldier being firmly escorted out of a cartoon house.

Ivy tried the explaining part on her little brother, who was building something meticulous out of crackers on the living room floor. "The First Amendment protects freedom of religion," she began, "freedom of speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government." He ate one of his walls and offered no follow-up questions. Ivy paced the hallway. This was the problem with the assignment: she could recite the list, but her own words kept turning into the textbook's words wearing a disguise.

She tested an idea. If she actually understood it, she should be able to spot it in the wild, the way you notice a word you just learned everywhere. She texted Peter, who ran the school paper and had spent Tuesday complaining that the principal wanted to preview the next issue. Ivy typed, "Peter, what protects the press in the United States?" His reply came fast: "Nothing, probably. He's going to read everything before we print it." She frowned. He was usually the person who knew things. The probability that Peter was wrong about something involving the paper seemed low, and yet.

She read the amendment a fourth time, tapping each line. Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof, or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press, or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the government for a redress of grievances. The press. Right there, in the actual First Amendment, third on the list. Peter had been looking at the principal's rules when he should have been looking at these. She called him back. "It's the First Amendment," she said. "Freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. That's what protects the press."

There was a pause long enough for Ivy to hear the printer starting on Peter's end. "Huh," Peter said. "Okay. I'm putting that in the editorial. With, you know, actual citations." Ivy went back to the kitchen table, folded her crumpled notes into a paper airplane, and aimed it at the recycling bin. It landed in the sink.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: The Northeast blackout that began on August 14, 2003, cut power to about 55 million people in parts of the northeastern United States and Ontario, Canada.
story:
The lights went out just as Nevaeh was about to put the macaroni in the microwave, and for a second she thought she had blown a fuse. She opened the back door and looked across the yard. Every house on the street was dark, and even the streetlight at the corner had gone out like someone had plucked it from the sky. She tried to evade the obvious conclusion by blaming her own house, but the whole street staring back at her, black and silent, made that impossible.

She texted Kassidy, whose battery was at four percent. "Power out at yours too?" Kassidy wrote back "yep" and then her phone died, which Kassidy would later describe as a radical betrayal by modern technology. Ten minutes later Kassidy and Harlow climbed over the low fence between the backyards, carrying a bag of chips and a board game that turned out to be useless without light.

"We can't just sit here doing nothing," Harlow said, flopping onto the grass. Nevaeh had an idea forming, though, one she wanted to test. Her grandmother had told her once about the big blackout of August 14, 2003, when she'd had to walk all the way home from work in the heat. "It wasn't just our city," Grandma had said. "It cut power to about 55 million people, across parts of the northeastern United States and Ontario, Canada." Nevaeh had looked it up afterward because 55 million sounded impossible, and it had checked out. Which meant that if tonight's outage was big enough, they might not be the only ones.

"Hand me the battery radio from the porch shelf," she said. Kassidy found it, and Nevaeh clicked it on, moving the dial past static until a calm voice said crews were working on an outage affecting several neighborhoods, including theirs. "See? It's not just us," Nevaeh said. "It's a pattern. One street going dark is a fuse. A whole region is something bigger, and the radio tells us which." Harlow sat up. "So the radio is like, blackout news for people with no phones."

They made a game of it while they waited, guessing when the power would come back. Harlow guessed forty minutes, Kassidy guessed ten, and Nevaeh said an hour, "because the repair work always slows down when it hits a plateau and nothing seems to be happening." At minute fifty-two the porch light snapped on and the microwave beeped in the kitchen as if it had been waiting to finish its job all along. Kassidy whooped so loudly that a neighbor's dog barked back from two yards over.

"That's my win," Nevaeh said, holding up the radio like a trophy.

"You said an hour," Harlow said.

"I said the plateau would eat up the last part. I was right about the plateau."

"Macaroni time," Kassidy announced, and the three of them headed for the kitchen, the radio still humming in Nevaeh's hand.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Each operation has an inverse that undoes it: subtraction undoes addition, and division undoes multiplication.
story:
The math Olympiad tryout sheets were supposed to circulate through the rows, but Kody grabbed his so fast he nearly ripped it. "The winner goes to the regional finals," he whispered. "Prestigious. Trophies, interviews, the whole thing. I need to make that team." Theodore took his own sheet and read the first problem: x + 7 = 12. His stomach did a small flip, part nerves, part thrill.

He stared at the equation. Somewhere under that equals sign, a number was hiding, and he wanted to dig it out. Adding seven had turned the mystery number into twelve. So what would undo adding seven? He tried subtraction, taking seven away from the twelve, and wrote x = 5. Then he tested it, sliding five back into the original: 5 + 7 really did equal 12. He almost knocked his pencil off the desk.

"That was fast," said Omer, leaning over from the next seat. "How'd you get it?"

"Subtraction undoes addition," Theodore said. "It's like the reverse gear."

Omer squinted at his own paper. Problem three was 4x = 20. "This one's multiplication. What undoes that?"

Theodore thought about it while tapping his pencil. If subtraction undoes addition, then maybe the opposite of multiplying was dividing. Omer split twenty by four and got five, then checked it: four times five made twenty. "It works!" Omer said, loud enough that Mr. Ferreira looked up from his desk and gave them a thumbs-up.

Problem five was 3x + 5 = 17, and that one looked like a locked door with two locks. Theodore reasoned out loud in a whisper. "The plus five is on the outside, so undo that first." He subtracted five from both sides and got 3x = 12. Then division, splitting both sides by three. x = 4. Two inverses, one after the other, and the hidden number had nowhere left to hide.

When the bell rang, Kody was still on problem six, chewing his pen. "Wait," he said, "you just did the same thing to both sides? Every time?"

"Every time," Theodore said. "That's the whole game."

Kody copied the idea down in the back of his notebook, pressing so hard the words showed through to the next page, right across the spine. "Tomorrow," he said, standing up, "we're both making that team."

"Race you to the tryouts," Theodore said, and he was already out the door.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Cooked rice can rest off the heat with the lid on for several minutes, which lets the trapped steam finish cooking it and frees the stove for other dishes.
story:
At seven o'clock on Saturday morning, Sadie laid out three burners behind her mother's stall at the farmers' market and felt like a general inspecting troops. The market manager had given her the corner spot for the young cooks' lunch hour, and the rules were posted on the pole: rice, a curry, and a flatbread, all served together at twelve, all judged by whoever wandered by with a fork.

She had never cooked all three at once. At home she had made them one at a time, which was like juggling one ball. Now she had three burners, one hour, and two friends who had shown up at dawn claiming they wanted to help. Maxence was measuring flour for the flatbread dough with the confidence of someone who had read half a recipe. Alexander was chopping onions for the curry and crying about it, quietly, so as not to seem weak.

The rice went on first, because rice took longest. At least, that was her theory. She had written her plan on the back of a market flyer: rice at 11:00, curry at 11:10, flatbread at 11:30. It looked scientific. It looked like a plan drawn by someone who knew things.

At 11:20, the rice pot started making its familiar burbling noise, and by 11:25 the water was gone and the grains looked done, which was bizarre to Sadie, because her flyer clearly said the rice should need twenty more minutes. The curry was still pale and thin. The flatbread was a ball of dough sleeping under a cloth, nowhere near a pan. She lifted the lid, stabbed a grain with a fork, and chewed it. Slightly crunchy in the middle. Not done. Also not not done.

"This is a disaster," she announced.

Alexander came over, still wiping his eyes, and peered into the pot. "My gran does this," he said. "Rice can rest off the heat with the lid on for several minutes. The trapped steam finishes cooking it."

"Off the heat?"

"Off the heat, lid on. Then your burner's free." He said it like he was reporting the weather, then went back to his onions.

Sadie looked at the empty third burner, then at her flyer, and revised the whole plan in her head. She slid the rice pot onto the back of the table, lid clamped down, and pulled the curry onto the now-free burner to bubble harder. The dough got rolled and slapped into a pan, and Maxence pressed bubbles into it with his thumb the way a man at another stall had shown him, because Maxence learned everything by watching strangers.

At 11:59, the curry had thickened, the flatbread was blistered and warm, and the rice, spooned into paper cups, was soft all the way through, no crunch anywhere. The steam had done its job in there, invisible, while she'd been busy. A line of customers had formed, holding forks the way people hold tickets.

The market manager came by at 12:01, tasted the curry, tasted the bread, and looked at the rice cup for a long moment. "Three entries or one dish?" he asked, pencil hovering over his clipboard, because the rules required the young cooks to submit them separately, and separate entries were judged separately, and there was only one prize.

"Three," said Sadie.

Maxence leaned toward her. "You know that means you're competing against yourself."

The manager's pencil touched the paper.

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: The India Meteorological Department gives June 1 as the normal date for the southwest monsoon to reach Kerala, on India's southwestern coast.
story:
James stopped at the bend in the trail where the trees opened up and the valley showed below, green and steaming after yesterday's rain. He unzipped his pack, pulled out the crumpled notecards for his geography presentation, and frowned at them. "I still don't get how to start," he said. "Mr. Mehta wants us to explain where the monsoon actually comes from, and all my cards just say 'air moves.' That's nothing."

Lionel, who was allergic to half the plants on this trail and had been complaining about his pollen allergy since the parking lot, sat down on a flat rock and wiped his nose. "Start with what your grandfather told you," he said. "You said he does something every year."

"He circles a date on the calendar," James said. "June 1. He lives in Kerala, on the southwest coast of India, and he says June 1 is the normal date for the monsoon to arrive there. The India Meteorological Department is the one that gives that date." He looked at the cards again. "But knowing the date doesn't explain the wind."

Pascal had been quiet, crouched at the edge of the rock where a thin stream slid over stone. He pulled off his boot, dumped out a pebble, and pointed at the water. "Watch this side. It's in the shade, and it's cold. Feel the rock on the sunny side." James pressed his palm against both. The sunny rock was warm enough that he could feel it through his skin; the shaded one was cool and damp.

"So the sun heats the land," James said slowly, turning it over. "And the land heats faster than the sea. If the air over warm land rises, then cooler, wetter air has to come in from the ocean to take its place. The wind would blow from the sea toward the coast. That's why it arrives on the southwest coast first." He grabbed his pencil and flipped a notecard over, sketching a curve of coast with arrows pushing inland. "That's the hidden part. You can't see the whole monsoon, you can only see the pieces."

The wind shifted just then, coming up the valley and flattening the grass in long silver lines, and a hawk above them tilted on it, riding the turbulent air in tight, uneasy circles. James held the notecard up so the sun shone through it, arrows and coast plainly visible.

"That's it," Pascal said. "Say that tomorrow, exactly like that."

"Rice needs the rain," James added, folding the card into his shirt pocket. "Whole farm seasons ride on that wind arriving when it should." He shouldered his pack, and the three of them started up the trail, James still talking, his hand tracing the path of the wind through the air ahead of him.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: Foreshadowing is a hint early in a story about something that will happen later, often noticed only on a second reading.
story:
The rain streaked the window of the reading nook, and Brody had until tomorrow morning to write a page about the story Ms. Okonkwo had assigned, a story about a farmer who watches his well run dry and then loses everything in a fire. He had read it twice and still had nothing. His notebook page said only "arid = dry, obviously," which was not going to earn him anything but a frown.

He texted Edie first. "What did you write about the fire story?" Her reply came back fast: "The part where the lantern flickers. Jared says it's important but he won't say why." Brody flipped through the story hunting for the lantern. There it was, in the last scene, tipped over in the barn. He almost closed the book, then stopped. He turned back to page one instead, just to check something, because Ms. Okonkwo had said one thing in class that kept circling back to him: foreshadowing, she'd called it, a hint early in a story about something that will happen later, often noticed only on a second reading. She hadn't explained more. She'd just smiled and moved on.

Page one. The farmer's daughter wipes dust off a lantern no one had lit in weeks. That was it. Brody sat forward so fast the cushion slid off the nook bench. The lantern was there on page one, quiet and ordinary, and the fire was waiting for it at the end. He tested the idea against the well next. First paragraph: the farmer jokes that the water level never seemed to diminish, not even in August. Then the well empties on page six. The story had been leaving a trail the whole time, and he had walked right over it on his first read.

He thought about last semester, when he'd handed in an essay about a different story and guessed at the ending's meaning, and Ms. Okonkwo had written "look back" in red pen at the top. He'd ignored it, or maybe he hadn't understood it. He understood it now, sitting cross-legged with pages ruffling under his thumb.

His phone buzzed. Edie again. "You find anything?"

"Page one," he typed. "The lantern and the well. They're hints. Check the first paragraph and then the ending."

A long pause, then three exclamation points. Brody pulled his notebook close and started writing, pen moving fast, while outside the rain kept falling and the last of the daylight began to diminish behind the neighbor's roof.

"Dead man's well," he muttered to himself, underlining the phrase twice. "Dead man's lantern."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Telling a trusted adult is not tattling when the goal is to protect someone from harm rather than to get someone in trouble.
story:
Levi had been watching the basketball courts from the top of the slide for three days, and by the third day he could see the pattern. Every recess, Tyson and two other boys waited until Syeda picked up a ball, and every recess they found a reason to take it from her or knock her shot off course. It was never one big thing. It was a dozen small things, so small that each one alone might look like nothing, and Syeda had stopped shooting altogether. She just stood near the fence now with her hands in her pockets.

"They'll call me a snitch," she said when Levi finally climbed down and stood beside her. "Tyson says anyone who reports him is a snitch, and then it gets worse."

Levi turned that over. At his old school he had been careful to sort every problem into a private category: things you handled yourself, and things you took to an adult, which everyone knew was the weaker move. But the sorting seemed wrong now. He had tried the playground fix on Monday, walking over and asking Syeda to be on his team, and Tyson had simply followed them and kept talking. Polite words did not make him stop.

"Think about it," Levi said slowly. "When you tell on someone just to get them in trouble, that's tattling. Telling a trusted adult isn't tattling when the goal is to protect someone from harm." He had heard something like that once, maybe from his grandmother, and had dismissed it. Now it seemed like an actual rule with an actual test you could apply, so he decided to test it. Mr. Nwosu ran the after-school program and kept a meticulous eye on the courts, tracking who played fair and who didn't, though he rarely said much during recess itself.

"If he does it again," Levi said, "I'm the one going to Mr. Nwosu. Not you. Watch what happens."

They didn't have to wait long. At the next recess Tyson took the ball out of Syeda's hands before she'd even dribbled it, and Levi walked straight across the blacktop. He kept his voice even, told Mr. Nwosu only what he had seen on all three days, and said that Syeda couldn't play because of it. Mr. Nwosu listened without interrupting, then crossed to the fence and spoke to Tyson quietly, away from everyone else.

Tyson came back with his jaw set, and for a minute Levi thought the plan had failed. But Tyson only bounced the ball once, hard, and looked over at Syeda. "You actually any good?" he called across the court. Syeda pulled her hands out of her pockets and stepped onto the paint.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Research on expert performers has found that how someone practices, focusing on specific weak spots, matters more than simply playing a piece many times.
story:
Benjamin had played "The Wandering Tune" nineteen times that Saturday, and his fingers still tripped in the same place every single time, measures eleven through fourteen, where the notes jumped up fast. He slumped on the piano bench in the living room and stared at the sheet music like it had personally insulted him.

His phone buzzed. It was a message from Addilyn: "You still stuck on that song? My sister had the same problem last year. Her teacher told her something weird. Research on expert performers found that how you practice, focusing on specific weak spots, matters more than just playing a piece a bunch of times. She stopped running the whole piece and drilled only the measures she kept missing. Won her recital." Benjamin read it twice. Nineteen full runs, and he had never once practiced only the hard part. He slid his finger under the four stubborn measures and marked them with a pencil.

He played nothing but measures eleven through fourteen. Slow, then slower, then fast, then slow again. His little brother wandered in halfway through, humming the four measures along with him until they were stuck in both their heads, which was annoying and also, somehow, helpful. After twenty minutes, Benjamin tried the whole song from the top, and his hands sailed through the jump like it had never been a problem at all. He laughed out loud, alone in the living room.

On Monday after school, he knocked on Mr. Bekele's door. The retired music teacher lived two houses down and had lent Benjamin the sheet music in the first place, excluding from his stack of books anything too advanced. "Did it go badly?" Mr. Bekele asked, seeing Benjamin's face. "No, the opposite," Benjamin said. "I finally fixed it. Four measures, over and over. Not the whole song." Mr. Bekele's grin was infectious, wide and sudden. "Ah, so you learned what most people take years to learn."

At Thursday's recital tryout, Benjamin watched Joaquin flub the same passage three times in a row and stare at his shoes afterward, his ears going red with embarrassment. Benjamin caught him in the hallway. "Which measures are you missing?" he asked. Joaquin showed him, and together they found an empty practice room. "Just these," Benjamin said, pointing at the page. "Nothing else. Watch." He played the four measures slowly, and Joaquin pulled out his clarinet and copied him, measure by measure, until the sun through the window turned orange.

At the end of the hour, Joaquin ran the piece from the beginning. When he hit the hard part and kept going, clean and easy, he looked up and said, "Play it again. I want to hear the whole thing."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Herman Snellen developed his eye chart of rows of shrinking letters in 1862.
story:
The letters on the wall kept going soft. Eleanor squinted at the chart from the plastic chair, and the bottom rows blurred into gray insects. Mya stood in the doorway of the nurse's office, holding both their hall passes like they were tickets to something.

"Read the smallest line you can," the nurse said.

Eleanor read down to the fourth row and stopped. "E, F, P, and then it just smears."

The nurse wrote something on a card. "You'll need an eye exam. You're around twenty-forty, maybe worse." She pulled the chart off its hook and turned it over, and Eleanor saw printing on the back, small and brown with age. "This old thing. I've been meaning to get a new one."

"Wait," Eleanor said, leaning over. "How old is it?"

The nurse tilted the card toward the light. "The print says the design dates to 1862. A Dutch doctor named Herman Snellen came up with it, rows of letters that shrink line by line. We've been squinting at his idea since before anyone's great-grandparents were born."

"That's ancient," Mya said. "That chart is older than the school. Older than the whole town, probably."

Eleanor stared at the fading E at the top, huge and confident, and something bothered her. "If it's that old, the letters might be worn. Maybe I can't read the bottom because it's faded, not because my eyes are bad." It sounded like an excuse the moment she said it, but she wanted to test it anyway. She formulated a quick plan. "Could I try reading something new? Same size, but printed fresh?"

The nurse raised an eyebrow, then smiled. "Sure." She took a sticky note and a marker and copied the smallest row's letters from the chart, P E C Z F, in bold black strokes, and taped the note beside the faded row.

Eleanor looked. The sticky-note letters stayed stubbornly smeared, exactly as blurred as the originals. Same letters, same size, new ink, still soft. It wasn't the chart. It was her eyes. She felt her face go warm, and Mya's hand landed briefly on her shoulder.

"Okay," Eleanor said quietly. "It's me."

Two weeks later she sat in the same chair while the nurse helped her unfold her new glasses, the frames a versatile shade of blue that the optician had promised worked with everything. The sticky note was still taped to the wall. Through the new lenses, P E C Z F stood up sharp and black and certain, every edge clean.

Mya grinned from the doorway. "Can you see the tundra project poster from here too? That's my true test."

Eleanor looked down the hall toward their classroom, where the frost-blue poster hung above the sink, and read the title across its top without a single squint. "Every word," she said. "Even the small print."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In France, friends often greet each other with cheek kisses called 'la bise', and the number of kisses varies from region to region.
story:
At Gage's front door, Maelie stood holding a box of store-bought cookies while his cousin Cecile swept toward her and kissed her right cheek, then her left. Maelie froze, her arms rigid, nearly bopping Cecile in the chin with the cookies. Behind Cecile came Gage's uncle, who kissed her cheek once, twice, three times, and stepped back beaming. Maelie's face burned. At her own house, guests got a wave and a "come in," and she had never once considered that her rules might not be the only ones.

"She does it to everyone," Gage whispered as they headed to the kitchen. "It's called la bise. My cousins do it like saying hi." Maelie set the cookies on the counter, where Gage's aunt took them with both hands and a small bow, and said something in French that made everyone laugh warmly. Maelie laughed too, though she had no idea what the joke was, and that felt like wearing someone else's coat.

At dinner she watched like a detective. Hands on the table, not in laps. Bread torn, never cut with the knife. Cecile said "bon appetit" before anyone lifted a fork, and even Gage's little brother waited. Maelie kept her wrists resting beside her plate and tore her bread carefully, and when she almost reached for the water pitcher before the uncle had been served, she caught herself and pretended to be very interested in the tablecloth. She was not going to be the defendant at dinner court, accused of guzzling water out of turn. That was silly, she knew. She still put the pitcher down.

After dinner she found Cecile alone on the porch steps and tested the question that had been bugging her all evening. "You kissed me twice, but your dad did three. Is he just, like, extra friendly?" Cecile tilted her head. "In his region, everyone does three. Where I live, it's two. It changes from place to place in France." So it was not about her at all. There was a system, a map of kisses she couldn't see, and she had spent the whole afternoon thinking the uncle liked her more than Cecile did. She had tried to decode faces and it had all been postcodes.

"It's two for me," Cecile said, standing and offering her hand like they were closing a deal. Maelie leaned in, right cheek first, and got it right this time, two soft kisses, one on each side. Cecile grinned and went inside. Gage appeared in the doorway, and Maelie raised her hand for a high five, but he laughed and kissed the air beside her cheek twice instead. Her hand hung there, useless and vain, while the porch light flicked on. "Next time," she said, "I'm doing three."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A reverse image search can show where a photo appeared online before, which can reveal that an old picture is being passed off as new.
story:
The rain hammering Mackenna's window should have been the most exciting thing in the house, but Scarlett couldn't stop staring at Mackenna's phone. Everyone in town was sharing the same photo: a street turned into a brown river, a mailbox sticking out of the water like a tiny lighthouse. The caption said the creek had burst its banks two blocks from the school.

"That's our street," Mackenna said, her grin infectious. "No school tomorrow, definitely."

Scarlett looked at the water again. Something about it itched at her, the way a word on the tip of your tongue does. The creek didn't flood fast. It crept. And that mailbox looked brand new, no rust, no stickers, when she knew every mailbox on Miller's street wore at least three bumper stickers and a coat of orange stains.

"Can I borrow your laptop?" she asked. "Two minutes. Scientific business."

Mackenna's older brother, sprawled on the couch, muttered, "It's real, it's on the news page."

"Pages can be wrong," Scarlett said. "A page is just a place. It's not proof." She carried the laptop to the kitchen table, saved the photo, and did the thing Miller had shown her back in September, when someone had passed off a shark in a swimming pool as their own pet. "Reverse image search," Miller had called it then, and she did it now: she fed the picture itself into the search bar and let it hunt.

The results bloomed across the screen. The same flood photo had appeared online years earlier, on a weather site, during a storm in a town three states away. It hadn't been taken yesterday, or here, at all.

"Whoa." Mackenna leaned over her shoulder. "So it's old?"

"Older than your mailbox theory," Scarlett said. "Somebody grabbed a dramatic picture and said it was new."

Mackenna's brother sat up. "Wait. People just share stuff because it looks true?"

"Looks true and is true are different animals," Scarlett said. "Kind of like how your dog looks innocent while the trash can is knocked over."

They spent the next hour checking. The photo of the gym with water at the doors was real; the reverse search found nothing older than that morning, and the school's own page confirmed it. The one of a canoe paddling down Main Street turned out to be from a festival four years back, when the town literally closed the street and handed out paddles for fun.

"So what's the criterion, then?" Mackenna asked, chewing a pretzel. "How do we decide which ones to send to the group chat?"

Scarlett considered. "If we can check it, we check it. If we can't, maybe we wait an hour. Boring wins."

"Boring never wins," Mackenna said, but she typed a correction to the group chat anyway: NOT OUR STREET. PHOTO IS FROM YEARS AGO. She added a jellyfish emoji holding a tiny magnifying glass, because, she said, the truth needed a mascot. Scarlett decided the jellyfish could symbolize the whole afternoon: weird, a little see-through, but stinging exactly when it should.

The actual rain kept falling, the actual creek kept creeping, and Mackenna's mom called up that they should check whether school posted anything official. Scarlett closed the laptop and looked out at the gray sheet of water on the glass. Somewhere out there, she thought, was the true story of today, patient as the creek, just waiting for somebody to go looking.

"Tomorrow," Mackenna said, "we fact-check the cafeteria menu."

"Everything," Scarlett agreed, "except the mystery meat. That one stays unsolved."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be tested against evidence and shown to be true or false, while an opinion expresses a belief, feeling or judgment that evidence cannot prove.
story:
Khalil leaned over the bean plants on the back counter and pointed at the two trays. "The ones under the red light grew more," he said. "That's a fact." Finnegan rolled his eyes so hard it looked painful. "No, it's your opinion. You just like the red light because it looks like a sci-fi movie."

Eli squinted at both trays. The beans under the red lamp did seem taller, but "seem" was doing a lot of work in that sentence. The science fair judging started in forty minutes, and their poster was supposed to answer a question with evidence, not with whoever argued loudest. Mr. Okonkwo had already stopped by once and asked, "How do you know?" Eli had said "you can just tell," and Mr. Okonkwo had smiled in a way that made Eli want a better answer.

"Maybe we can measure them," Eli said, pulling a ruler out of the drawer. Khalil grabbed his wrist. "We don't have time, the poster isn't even done." "We have forty minutes," Eli said. "Measuring takes five." Finnegan, who had been drawing a volcano on the corner of the poster that had nothing to do with beans, said, "Fine, but if we demolish our whole layout to write numbers on it, that's on you." He said it while sliding the ruler toward Eli, which meant he agreed.

They measured all twelve plants under each lamp and wrote the heights on the board. The red-light beans averaged taller, but two of them were shorter than any of the others, which surprised Khalil. "So I was right," he said. "Sort of," Eli said. "You said they grew more. Now we can actually check it. That makes it a claim, not just something you feel." Finnegan tapped the poster. "So when I say the volcano drawing makes it look awesome, that's different? Nobody could measure that?" "Right," Eli said. "That one's an opinion. Evidence can't prove it true or false. It's just what you believe." Finnegan looked wounded. "It is awesome. That part is authentic volcano shading, I looked at pictures."

With twelve minutes left, they copied the numbers onto the poster and Khalil wrote the heading Results while Finnegan, grudgingly and carefully, colored his volcano smaller so it wouldn't look like propaganda for volcanoes in a bean experiment. When Mr. Okonkwo came back and read the chart, he asked again, "How do you know?" Eli pointed at the ruler and the two rows of numbers. "We checked," he said, and Mr. Okonkwo nodded once and moved on to the next table, where a girl was insisting that her crystals were the sparkliest in the class.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book 'Continuing Bonds' argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving.
story:
After the funeral, everyone gathered in Grandma's back yard under the big maple, the same tree Carter's grandfather had planted the year he and Grandma bought the house. Carter stood near the picnic table with his hands in his pockets, feeling the old watch on his wrist where it had been all morning. He had taken it from Grandpa's dresser two days ago, before anyone could pack it away. Now he wondered if that had been a mistake, if wearing it meant he was refusing to let go the way a person was supposed to.

He found Claire by the fence, poking at a beetle with a stick. She had come with her mom, and she was clearly bored, which was fair, since she had never even met Grandpa. "You okay?" she asked, glancing at the watch. "You keep looking at it like it might explode."

"Do you think it's weird, wearing this?" Carter asked. "Like, not moving on?" Claire shrugged, so he kept going. "My dad keeps saying we all have to move forward. I don't want to take it off, though. It still ticks."

Claire's face changed the way it did when she was about to win an argument in class. "My mom reads all this psychology stuff. There's a book called Continuing Bonds, from 1996, and it says keeping a connection to someone who died, with memories or objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving. She made me read the first chapter for a report." She said it fast, like she was reciting, then added, "So no, I don't think it's weird. I think it's science."

Carter turned the watch over. The case back was scratched from years of resting on Grandpa's workbench, next to the laser level he used when he built the porch. Every cousin had resented having to hold that board steady while the red line crawled across it, and now Carter would have given anything to hold it one more time. Maybe missing someone was inevitable, and maybe the watch was not a chain, just a bridge. He could test that. If he set it to the correct time and wore it to school tomorrow, and it felt like carrying Grandpa with him instead of hiding from the world, then Claire's book was right about him.

He worked the little crown with his thumbnail until the hands matched his phone. "It's set," he said. "Nine forty-two." Across the yard, his dad was stacking paper plates, and Carter walked over and held out his wrist without a word. His dad looked at the watch, then at him, and put one hand briefly on Carter's shoulder. "He'd be glad it still runs," his dad said. "Wear it to dinner."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer; around December 21, it is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn.
story:
Joseph had a globe on his desk, a flashlight, and one night to figure out the seasons before his presentation in Ms. Brennan's class. He had gotten the first part easily enough: Earth's axis was tilted, and the tilt caused the seasons. But when Diya had quizzed him at lunch, she asked why the tilt mattered, and his answer had come out as a jumble. "You said 'the Sun is more direct' about six times," she had said. "What does that even mean?" Now he stared at the globe and its two dotted lines, one above the equator and one below, and wondered what they marked.

He spun the globe slowly. The northern dotted line crossed Mexico, Africa, and India. The southern one ran through Australia and South America. He knew the equator, but these two lines had names, and he could not remember them, which was exactly the kind of thing Ms. Brennan would ask. He texted Khloe, who owned every book in the school library's astronomy section.

She called back within two minutes. "They're the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn," she said. "The one north of the equator is Cancer. Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. Around December 21, it's directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn." Joseph wrote it down, then read it back to her. "Wait, that's it," he said. "That's the whole thing I was missing."

He grabbed the flashlight and propped a book under the globe to keep it stable so it wouldn't roll off the desk. Then he held the flashlight level with the northern line and traced the beam. At that height, the light hit the Tropic of Cancer straight on, but everywhere north of it, the beam struck the globe at a slant, spreading thin and dim. He crouched down and slid the flashlight lower, level with the southern line, and watched the bright spot jump to the other side of the world. It was like the Sun was taking turns standing over each line, six months apart.

The next morning he found Diya at her locker. "Test me," he said. "Ask me why the tilt matters." She raised an eyebrow, game as always. "Fine. Why?"

He held up his hands like a globe and a Sun. "Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. That's where the light comes in straight and piles up, so it's summer there. Around December 21, it's directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn instead, and everything north of it only gets slanted light. Slanted light spreads out. It's like the beam on my globe last night, wide and weak." Diya nodded slowly. "Okay, that actually made sense."

In class, Ms. Brennan asked for volunteers, and Joseph's hand went up before he could talk himself out of it. He walked to the globe, pointed to the two dotted lines, and said the dates plainly, the way Khloe had said them to him. Ms. Brennan asked one follow-up question about the beam spreading out, and he answered it with the flashlight demo, sweeping the light across the tilted globe while the class leaned forward.

Afterward Diya bumped his shoulder in the hallway. "Good simile, by the way," she said. "The wide, weak beam. It contributed." Joseph laughed and shoved his notes back in his binder, already thinking about what he might present next time.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A baking soda volcano erupts because baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) reacts with vinegar (acetic acid) to produce carbon dioxide gas.
story:
Jordan had promised his science fair table would not be "just another volcano." By Saturday morning, the volcano itself was done, a lumpy gray cone of salt dough with a film canister buried in its throat, and the actual problem was still unsolved: every test eruption so far had been either a sad fizz or a blob of foam on the ceiling. He sat at the kitchen table with three measuring cups, a bottle of vinegar, and a box of baking soda, devising a plan that would make his project different from the twenty other volcanoes in the gym.

"Are you doing science or making salad dressing?" Lena asked, dropping into the chair across from him. She peered at his notebook, where he had drawn a table with columns for amounts and eruption height.

"Both, kind of," Jordan said. "Watch. Same amount of baking soda each time. Only the vinegar changes." He filled the first cup with a quarter cup of vinegar and dumped it into the canister.

The volcano produced a small burp of pink foam. Lena clapped once, in slow motion, to honor the effort.

"That's the control problem," Angelo said from the doorway, where he had appeared holding a cookie he clearly intended to eat over Jordan's project. "The foam isn't stable. It slides down before you can measure anything."

Jordan ignored the cookie situation and poured half a cup of vinegar for the second trial. This time the foam climbed the slope and actually reached the rim of the paper plate he had placed below. He wrote down the height. One full cup, in the third trial, sent foam over the plate's edge and onto Angelo's sleeve, which Angelo accepted as the cost of participation. The numbers in Jordan's table made a pattern, and he could see it clearly: more vinegar, bigger eruption, every single time.

"So why does it do that?" Lena asked, wiping foam off her elbow.

"My mom said it last night when she was reading my notes," Jordan said. "Baking soda, which is sodium bicarbonate, reacts with vinegar, which is acetic acid, and makes carbon dioxide gas. The gas is what pushes the foam out." He tapped his table of results. "So the factor that matters is how much vinegar I add. More vinegar, more gas, more mess."

"Your mom sounds like she wants a volcano of her own," Angelo said, shaking off his sleeve.

They ran a fourth trial just to be sure, and this time they laid down three paper plates, which turned out to be exactly two plates too few. From the doorway, Mr. Rivera, who had come over to borrow a ladder and never got around to mentioning it, said quietly, "Ceiling again?"

Jordan looked up at the new foam constellation and wrote "trial five: outdoors" in his notebook.

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: When two CSS rules of equal specificity set the same property, the one written later wins; this ordering is part of the cascade in Cascading Style Sheets.
story:
Ivy's web page had a heading that refused to stay in the middle. She had typed text-align: center into her CSS, exactly the way the handout showed, and for one glorious second the words "Ivy's Guide to the Lake Ecosystem" sat right in the middle of the screen. Then she saved the file, refreshed the browser, and the heading slid stubbornly back to the left.

"The tech showcase starts in twenty minutes," said Miles, leaning over from the next laptop. "Ms. Park wants everybody's page up on the big screen."

"I know." Ivy scrolled through her CSS again. There it was, near the top: h1 { text-align: center; }. It was spelled right. She had checked three times. So why did the heading act like she'd never written anything at all?

Neveah wandered over with her own laptop, chewing the last of a granola bar. "Ms. Park said those are more nutritious than the vending machine stuff, but I'm not sure I believe her." She glanced at Ivy's screen. "Still stuck?"

"Watch this," Ivy said. She deleted the word center, retyped it, saved, and refreshed. The heading stayed left, like it was ignoring her on purpose. "The computer is doing something I can't see. There has to be a rule somewhere."

"Maybe it's the page itself," Miles offered. "Like something in the HTML?"

Ivy shook her head. "The HTML worked before lunch. It was centered then." She stopped. It had worked before lunch. What had she done after lunch? She scrolled down through the stylesheet, past the paragraph styles, past the list styles, all the way to the bottom, where she'd added a new section while the other campers were at the lake.

There it was: h1 { text-align: left; }, sitting at the very end of the file.

"You wrote it twice," Neveah said, peering closer.

"I forgot." Ivy stared at the two rules, one at the top and one at the bottom, both aimed at the same heading. The bottom one was winning. But why the bottom? She moved the left rule up above the center rule, saved, and refreshed. The heading stayed left. She moved it back down. The heading went left again. Up, it centered. Down, it went left. It wasn't magic and it wasn't random. When two CSS rules of equal specificity set the same property, the one written later won.

"That's why they call it a cascade," Ivy said, mostly to herself. "The stuff at the end pours over everything before it."

"Ten minutes," Miles warned.

Ivy deleted the left rule entirely. The heading snapped to the center and stayed there. She used the last minutes to modify her list styles, adding a little space between the lines, and to drop in a photo of a turtle she'd taken on Monday. The page looked like a real page now.

When Ms. Park's projector lit up the mess hall wall, Ivy's turtle photo glowed and the heading sat dead center above it. Neveah elbowed her and whispered, "Best one so far."

Ivy grinned and hit refresh one more time, just to watch the heading stay put.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: In email, BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy': people added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.
story:
The group chat lit up at 9:04 with a screenshot from Dana: an email sent to the whole class by mistake, sixty addresses crowded into the To field like a bus packed past the doors. "Great," Dana typed. "Now everyone has my email." Someone had already forwarded it to a chat called "everyone but Dana," which was exactly as biased as it sounded, and Dana's replies had gone from jokes to one long silence. Nicholas stared at the screen. His own birthday invitation was sitting in his drafts folder, addressed the same careless way, and his stomach did a slow flip.

He typed into the group chat: "Does anyone know how to send something to a lot of people without showing everybody's address?" Camila answered fast, the way she did when she actually knew something. "Use BCC," she wrote. "BCC means blind carbon copy. People you put there get the message, but the other recipients can't see their addresses." Nicholas read it twice. He had always thought BCC was some grown-up office button, like CC's serious older cousin, not a door you could actually walk through.

Before he trusted it, he tested it. He sent a dummy email to his own address in the To field, with Camila's address tucked into BCC, and a note that said only "checking something." Then he walked to the kitchen, got a glass of water, and came back to two copies in his inbox. His own copy showed just his address. Camila's reply arrived seconds later: "I can see the email but not anyone else you sent it to. Also this is the weirdest invite I've ever gotten."

He exhaled, long and slow, and opened the real draft. He pasted the class list into the BCC field, one careful line at a time, and typed a short message about Saturday, two o'clock, pizza and games at his house. In the To field, the only name left was his own. It felt strange, like being a diplomat carrying sealed letters instead of shouting announcements down the hallway, but strange in a good way.

He hit send, then went back to the group chat, where Dana had finally posted again, a single shrug emoji. Nicholas typed: "Dana, check your inbox. And everybody, your addresses are safe with me." The typing bubble appeared under Dana's name, disappeared, appeared again. Then it landed: "Okay. What time on Saturday?"

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: In Canada's 2015 federal election, the Liberal Party won 184 of 338 seats, a majority, with about 39.5 percent of the popular vote.
story:
Jace set the shoebox ballot box on the folding table in the city hall lobby and counted the vote slips a third time, because the numbers refused to make sense. His class had been invited to run a mock election for a community open house, and Mr. De Vries had left him in charge of tallying results for the afternoon demonstration. The vote was simple: three imaginary parties, the reds, the blues, and the greens, competing for five seats.

"Okay," said Yann, leaning over his shoulder. "Reds won every seat."

"That's the problem." Jace spread the slips into piles. "Look. Reds got thirty-one votes out of a hundred. Blues got twenty-nine. Greens got forty. The greens actually won the most votes, but the reds took all five seats because their votes were packed into every district." He tapped the district map they had drawn on butcher paper. "Under our rules, whoever gets the most votes in each district wins that seat. Everything else counts for nothing."

Clovis arrived with hot chocolate from the lobby cart and slid one across the table to Jace without being asked, because she had noticed him rubbing his cold hands together. "So change the rules," she said.

"I can't just change them. That's not how it works."

"Then show both ways."

Jace stared at her. She was right. He flipped the butcher paper over and drew a second table, dividing the hundred votes by twenty, so each seat should represent twenty voters. The greens, with forty votes, earned two seats. The blues got one, the reds got one, and the last seat he split by remainder, which took some arguing until Yann and Clovis both agreed the blues were closer. Five seats, three parties represented. He labeled the two tables: first past the post, and proportional representation.

While they taped the paper to the display board, Jace remembered the evening last fall when his mother had let him stay up to watch the real election results roll in. He had pulled up a results page on her laptop and squiggled his finger down the columns, comparing the seat count with the vote percentages, and something had snagged in his mind. He had called his grandfather long distance just to ask about it. One party had won 184 seats out of 338, a majority of the House of Commons, with about 39.5 percent of the popular vote. Fewer than four voters in ten, and they ran the whole show. He had sat with that for a long time before going to bed.
