When the open house visitors began drifting past, an older woman stopped at the board and studied the two tables. "So this is why people argue about voting systems," she said.

"The green voters would cooperate better under the second one," Yann said, pointing. "Their votes actually add up to something."

Mr. De Vries came by at closing, read both tables top to bottom, and clapped Jace on the shoulder. "The logic holds," he said. "Bring the butcher paper to class on Monday. It's more durable than it looks."

Jace rolled it up carefully and tucked it under his arm like something worth keeping.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: When interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall, because buyers can get new bonds that pay more interest.
story:
Alicia slid her simulation packet across the lab table and read the assignment line again. "Compare a stock and a bond. Explain which is riskier and why." Ms. Jung had set up the whole classroom as a pretend market, with each student holding an envelope of paper assets, and she had just announced that interest rates had risen.

"That's not fair," said Mabel, who sat beside her under the paper canopy of leaves taped to the ceiling for the economics unit. "I already traded for my stuff." Mabel was trying to earn the best grade in the class because her older brother had gotten one, and Alicia knew it, so she passed her friend a highlighter before anything else, because Mabel always forgot hers.

Alicia opened her envelope. She owned one share of Graffiti Robot Company stock, which the market sheet said had jumped in price, and one bond from the city that paid its holder four dollars of interest each round. She had been planning to sell the bond for its face value, ten dollars, and buy a second share of stock. Ayden, at the next table, was shouting that he would pay twelve for any robot stock, and his voice seemed to transmit through the entire room, because suddenly everyone wanted stock and nobody was talking about bonds at all.

She walked to Ayden's table anyway. "Bond for sale. Ten dollars, like the face value says."

"Ten?" Ayden frowned at his market sheet. "The teacher just raised the interest rate. New bonds pay more than four dollars now. Why would I pay ten for yours when I can get a brand new one that pays more?" He offered her seven. She refused and tried the cashier station, then the cluster near the window. Everyone said some version of the same thing. Nobody would pay full price for her old bond, because buyers could get new bonds that paid more interest, and by the last round the best offer she received was six dollars.

Back at her table, she laid out both assets side by side. "Okay," she said slowly, mostly to herself. "My stock went up. My bond went down, and it fell because rates rose, not because the city stopped paying. So the stock could crash to nothing if the company fails, but the bond only dropped a few dollars and still pays interest every round." She had started the day certain that bonds were the safe, boring choice that nobody smart would pick. Now she scribbled on her comparison sheet, crossed out her first sentence, and wrote that each one was risky in a different way, and that a bond's price could fall even when nothing was wrong with it.

Ms. Jung rang the bell for presentations. Mabel leaned over. "So which is riskier?" she whispered.

"Watch this," Alicia said, and stood up holding both pieces of paper above her head like evidence. "Last round, my bond was worth less than it said on its face. I'm going to tell you exactly why."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: In bear country, parks such as Yosemite count anything with a scent as 'food', so toothpaste, sunscreen and trash must go in the bear locker too.
story:
The trail to the campground was humid, and Audrey's backpack strap stuck to her shoulder like tape. Behind her, her dad argued with her little brother about whether chips counted as a snack or a meal. Ahead, their neighbor from the next campsite, Mr. Qureshi, was already wrestling with a metal box bolted to a post.

"That's the bear locker," Angelique said, catching up. She and her family had arrived at the park the day before, and she had appointed herself tour guide. "Everything goes in there."

"Everything like food," Audrey said.

"Everything," Angelique repeated, and dropped her toothbrush and a tube of sunscreen through the steel door.

Audrey eyed the locker. She had heard about bears her whole life, sort of, in a vague way, the way she'd heard about quicksand. It had never mattered before. Now she stood in a pine forest in a national park where the ranger at the entrance had a clipboard and a serious face, and it mattered a lot. That night, a bear could walk through the campground. She felt a slow creep of dread in her stomach, which was ridiculous, because she was twelve and not afraid of toothpaste.

But that was the thing. She couldn't stop thinking about the toothpaste.

Their first evening, Audrey unpacked the family's food into the locker while her dad set up the tent. She put in the bread, the peanut butter, the trash bag, even the empty wrapper her brother had dropped in the dirt. Then she went back to the tent and stood there holding her toiletry kit, thinking. Angelique had said everything. The ranger pamphlet in the car had said something too. She'd skimmed it, and now she dug it out of the door pocket and read it again, properly this time.

"Anything with a scent counts as food," she read out loud.

"So sunscreen," said a voice. Keagan, Angelique's other friend from the site next door, had wandered over with a bag of marshmallows he was clearly not supposed to have. "Sunscreen, toothpaste, trash. All of it. Basically if a bear could smell it, it's dinner."

"That's grim," Audrey said.

"That's Yosemite rules," Keagan said, and shrugged. "My mom made me put my gum in there."

Audrey marched her whole kit back to the locker: toothpaste, chapstick, the little bottle of bug spray. When she got back, her dad was climbing into the tent with a look of bliss.

"I'm sleeping," he announced.

"Did you put your stuff in the locker?" Audrey asked.

"I don't have food."

"Sunscreen counts. Toothpaste counts. Trash counts."

He groaned the groan of a man who had driven six hours and now had to walk forty more feet. He went anyway, muttering, and came back smelling faintly of citronella and defeat.

The next morning they found muddy prints near the trash barrels two sites down, big ones, and a family standing around a tipped-over cooler looking miserable. Angelique nudged Audrey.

"Told you," she said.

"You're a regular bear diplomat," Audrey said.

"I'm the reason you still have a tent."

Audrey looked at the prints one more time, then went to double-check the locker. Everything with a scent, locked in steel, right where it belonged.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: A soliloquy is a speech in which a character, usually alone on stage, speaks their private thoughts aloud so the audience can hear them.
story:
The bus smelled of rain and vinyl seats, and Brielle had the last row to herself until Amina slid in beside her with a paperback held open like a tray. "Ms. García says we have to paraphrase the whole scene by Friday," Amina said, "into words people actually use." She tapped the page, where a Scottish king was busy thinking about murder.

Brielle read the speech slowly, mouthing the words. "If it were done when 'tis done, then 'twere well it were done quickly." She tried it out loud. "If it was over the moment I did it, I'd better do it fast." That much worked. But something bothered her. Macbeth was saying he wanted to kill Duncan, and there was nobody else in the scene. Lady Macbeth had just left the stage. So who was he talking to? She turned the pages back and forth, checking who had spoken last, checking the stage directions, and found only the word "alone."

"Wait," Brielle said, and recounted the scene to Amina from the top: the king arrives, the guests go to bed, Lady Macbeth exits, and then Macbeth just talks. To the air. "It's a soliloquy," Amina said. "That's what Ms. García called it this morning. The character is usually alone on stage, saying their private thoughts out loud so the audience can hear them." Brielle stared at the page. So the audience was the only witness. Macbeth was telling them a secret he could never tell a living soul, because anyone who heard it would know he was a traitor.

She tested the idea on the next speech. When Lady Macbeth came back and Macbeth said "we will proceed no further in this business," he lied to her face, smooth and stable as anything. But the audience already knew, from the soliloquy, exactly what he wanted and how much he doubted himself. That was the trick of it. The private speech was where the truth lived. She had thought the assignment was about translating old words. It was really about overhearing. She began to write in the margin of her notebook, quick and certain now: He tells us what he won't tell her.

Amina leaned over to read it, and the bus swayed around the corner by the stable yard, where the horses stood nose to nose under the wet roof. "You're ahead of me," Amina said. "I'm still stuck on half these words." Brielle flipped back to the first page of the scene. "Then we've got the whole ride," she said, and clicked her pen. "Start at the top."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Endowing means giving your partner a role or trait through what you say, as in 'Doctor, my arm hurts', which makes them the doctor.
story:
The community theatre smelled of dust and old velvet, and the stage lights buzzed so loudly William could hear them from the front row. Ms. Lawson had written two words on the chalkboard in the wing: yes, and. "Whatever your partner gives you," she said, "you take it and add to it. No blocking, no arguing. We'll go until the scene ends itself."

William's hands went cold. Last summer, at the talent show, he had frozen so completely that Darcy later told him he looked like he was trying to hibernate standing up. Forty seconds of silence, then the microphone squealed. He did not want that again, but he had signed up for this class anyway, because the poster said everyone gets better, and he wanted to believe a poster for once.

Darcy went first with Jeremie. "This elevator is stuck," Darcy said, yanking at an imaginary door. "Yes, and we've been in here since Tuesday," Jeremie answered, "so I've already eaten your sandwich." The audience laughed. Ms. Lawson called it good agreement, and the class nodded, reaching consensus without a word.

Then a girl went up and just stood there, staring at the boards. William recognized the frozen look. Her partner scanned the empty stage, then suddenly pointed and said, "Captain, the iceberg is straight ahead!" The girl snapped to life. "Full reverse!" she barked. "Sound the alarm!" William leaned forward. Something had changed her, and it wasn't courage. She had been nobody standing on boards, and then one sentence made her somebody.

"Anyone know what that's called?" Ms. Lawson asked. "Endowing," said Jeremie. "Like, you give your partner a role by what you say. 'Doctor, my arm hurts' makes them the doctor." Ms. Lawson snapped her fingers and pointed to the next pair.

William's turn came fast. He walked out under the transparent gel that turned the light pale blue, and his mind went blank the way it always did, cold and total. His mouth opened. He tried to think of a line and found nothing. His partner, a boy he didn't know, waited, then opened his own mouth, and William saw the freeze spreading.

So William spoke first, at his partner, fast. "Doctor, my arm hurts. It got worse after the whale swallowed us."

The boy blinked, then straightened like a man with ten years of medical school behind him. "Yes, and I told you not to pet the whale, William."

"You told me nothing, Doctor. You were asleep."

The class cracked up, and William felt his feet actually on the boards, warm and planted, and reached for the next line.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 1 of the Canadian Charter says its rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
story:
The town hall smelled of coffee and damp umbrellas, and Nicolas smoothed his notecards for the tenth time on the folding table. His class had been invited to speak about the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and Ms. Rosen had told him his part was simple: read one right and explain it in his own words. Simple was not the word Nicolas would have chosen. His hands still felt cold from the walk over, even though the room was warm.

A boy from another school, taller, with a lanyard swinging from his neck, grabbed the microphone first. "Freedom of expression," he announced, "means anyone can say anything they want, anywhere, anytime, and nobody can stop them." A few adults clapped. Nicolas felt his stomach tighten, because that was exactly what he had written on his card, in his own handwriting, underlined twice.

Aminata leaned over from the next chair. "Can I see your cards?" she whispered. When he handed them over, she flipped to the back, where he'd copied a section of the Charter for reference, and stood up. "Sorry," she said into the microphone, her voice steadier than Nicolas expected. "Section 1 of the Charter says its rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society." She read it slowly, then sat down, cheeks pink.

The lanyard boy frowned. "So the rights aren't really rights?" Nicolas stared at his card, and something clicked, like a pattern he'd been staring at without seeing. If the rights were absolute, they would run into each other, one person's freedom crashing into another's safety. The limits weren't a wall against the rights; they were the thing that let the rights work at all. He tested the idea in his head, turning it over the way he turned a puzzle piece before snapping it in. When Ms. Rosen nodded at him, he walked to the microphone.

"Freedom of expression means I can say what I believe," Nicolas said, "and other people can oppose me, out loud, and neither of us gets punished. It's not a hierarchy where the loudest voice wins. It's more like a tranquil lake that everyone gets to drink from, as long as nobody poisons it." The room laughed softly at the lake, and the lanyard boy actually smiled. Afterward, Aminata found him by the cookie table and pushed a napkin with two oatmeal cookies toward him. "You changed your card," she said. "I saw you cross it out." Nicolas bit into the cookie and pointed at the microphone stand, where the lanyard boy was now writing something down, crossing it out, starting again.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, is marked by lighting small oil lamps called diyas and is usually celebrated over five days.
story:
Gabrielle balanced the last clay lamp on her grandmother's windowsill and stepped back to inspect the row. Her elbow knocked two of them sideways, and she caught one before it rolled off the ledge entirely.

"Careful," her grandmother said from the kitchen, laughing. "Those are diyas."

"Diyas," Gabrielle repeated, setting the little lamp upright. "Small oil lamps. Got it." She counted them anyway, because the whole afternoon had turned into a job with rules. Nine along the living room window, seven along the bedroom one, and the wicks still had to be checked before dark.

Jeremi and Fernando arrived just as the sky outside went purple, their bikes dropped in the courtyard like the riders had been flung off. Jeremi had never been to a Diwali celebration before and stood squinting at the windowsill as if it were a puzzle.

"Wait," he said. "Your grandma puts fire on the ledge and just... trusts nobody knocks it over? My dad won't even let me light a candle because of the mortgage papers on the desk."

"It's Diwali," Fernando said, tickling a mosquito bite on his arm. "Festival of lights. My family does it too, but we don't put them all in one window."

Gabrielle picked up one of the diyas and turned it in her hand. "The lights go out at night sometimes," she said. "Yesterday the one in the kitchen guttered out, and today the ones by the door. I keep thinking there's a reason, like a pattern." She narrowed her eyes at the window. "The kitchen one is right under the vent. The door ones are where the draft comes in when it opens."

"So the wind blows them out, genius," Jeremi said.

"That's a guess. I want to verify it." Gabrielle slid two lamps away from the drafty corner and placed them closer together near the middle of the ledge. "If these two stay lit longer than the ones I left in the corner, then it's the draft."

Her grandmother came out with a box of matches, chuckling at the three of them crouched at the window like detectives. She lit each wick, one by one, and the humid evening air began to smell faintly of oil and smoke.

"Five days of this," she said, shaking the match out. "You'll have plenty of time to watch your lamps."

"Five whole days," Jeremi whispered, as though the lamps themselves might hear him and get ideas.

They all sat on the floor below the ledge, watching the small flames bend and steady. In the corner, the leftmost diya flickered, sputtered, and went dark.

Gabrielle pointed at it. "Exhibit A."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water should never be poured on a grease fire, because it turns to steam instantly and spreads the burning oil; turning off the heat and covering the pan with a lid smothers it.
story:
Emilia had claimed the camp stove the way explorers claim mountains, which meant she stood in front of it with a spatula and refused to let anyone else touch the frying pan. Dinner was her job tonight, all of it, and she'd planned to prove she could handle the whole category of outdoor cooking, from soup to dessert, without a single adult hovering.

"Hovering," her dad said, hovering.

"See? That's the word. You're doing it." She pointed the spatula at the picnic table where Chloe and Meadow sat sorting marshmallows by size, a project Meadow insisted was scientific. "Go sit with them."

He drifted a few steps back, but not far, and Emilia poured oil into the pan for the flatbread she'd been practicing all week. The oil heated, shimmered, and then, when she nudged the pan to even it out, a tongue of flame leapt up from the surface. Chloe yelped. Meadow dropped a marshmallow.

Emilia's first instinct was the blue water jug sitting right there by the stove. Her hand actually went for it before her brain caught up. Two summers ago, Mr. Nasser, their neighbor, had been frying plantains in his driveway when his pan flared exactly like this, and she had watched him calmly reach past the water pitcher and slide a lid over the flames instead. He'd said only one sentence at the time, mostly to himself: "Never pour water on a grease fire." She'd asked why once, later, and he'd shrugged and said the flames would only get bigger, so a lid and no heat was the answer.

So Emilia grabbed the pan's lid, not the jug, slid it over the top, and shut off the burner with a click. The fire underneath dwindled, sulked, and went out, leaving a thin trail of smoke curling from under the rim.

"Whoa," said Meadow. "Why not the water?"

"Water would've made it way worse," Emilia said. "Lid and no heat. That's the move." She lifted the lid a crack, peeked in, and set it back down. "Also, we're having soup."

Her dad let out a breath that sounded like a laugh trapped on its way out. "I wasn't hovering."

"You were hovering at a distance," Chloe said. "There's a whole category for that. Long-range hovering."

"I'm biased," he admitted, holding up his hands, "because my daughter just put out a fire and didn't burn the flatbread." He peered over her shoulder as she lifted the lid again. The pan was scorched but fine. The oil was still hot enough to sizzle when she dropped in the first piece of dough, and it puffed up golden at the edges, perfectly ordinary, as if flames had never happened.

Emilia slid the flatbread onto a plate and held it out. "Dinner, family. Fire show included, no extra charge."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: If Earth's axis had no tilt, sunlight would hit each place at the same angle all year, so there would be almost no seasons.
story:
The envelope from Mackenzie was waiting in Asher's backpack when he got to the science museum, and he read it twice while Emerson queued for tickets. "I heard Ms. Virtanen is picking two people to present at the assembly," Mackenzie had written, "and I think it should be you. But you'd better actually understand the seasons, because she'll ask questions in front of everyone. Last year I froze up there and I still think about it." Asher folded the letter carefully. He had said yes to the assembly without really knowing why, and the doubt had followed him all week like a shadow.

The exhibit hall held a giant model of the sun and a rack of globes with little lamps you could wheel around them. A sign challenged visitors: Make winter happen. Asher picked up a globe and started to walk it around the sun, watching the lamp, but nothing changed. The light hit the northern half the same way at every step of the circle.

"You're holding it wrong," Emerson said, though she sounded unsure. She wanted her turn with the globe, and she wanted to be the one who figured it out first; she kept grabbing the base and turning it toward her. Asher held on. He remembered a diagram from the curriculum binder Ms. Virtanen had lent him, one he'd skimmed on the bus. A slanted line through the planet. He tipped the globe sideways, leaning it as he walked the circle, and stopped.

"Look at this spot," he said, pointing at a dot painted near the top of the globe. When the leaning globe was on one side, the dot caught the lamp's light at a shallow, glancing angle. Halfway around, the same dot faced the beam almost straight on. He kept the tilt steady and monitored the dot through a full lap, holding his phone camera up to record it so he could check later. Then, to be sure, he set the globe perfectly upright and walked it around again. The light hit the dot at the same angle every single time. Winter and summer never came. "It's the tilt," he said. "If Earth's axis had no tilt, sunlight would hit each place at the same angle all year. There'd be almost no seasons."

Emerson leaned over his phone, watching the recording with an infectious grin spreading across her face. "Say that again," she said, reaching for the globe. "Say it slow, and this time let me hold the tilt."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a blind test, participants do not know which sample is which, so their expectations cannot sway their answers.
story:
Paisley dragged the folding table to the middle of the garage and wiped off a smudge of motor oil with an old rag. On Saturday she would tell twenty classmates which cereal tasted better, the name brand or the store brand, and she wanted the answer to be real. Her dad's workbench smelled like sawdust and cold metal, and through the half-open door she could hear a sprinkler ticking across the lawn.

Gibson arrived first, carrying two boxes in a paper bag so nobody on the street could read the labels. "I got the same kind," he said, setting them down. "Toasted oat rings, both of them. One costs almost double." Lia came next with a notebook and a box of small plastic bowls. She lined them up in two parallel rows along the table edge, matched pairs, white and identical.

"Here's the problem," Paisley said. "My brother swears the expensive one tastes better, but he always knows which bowl it's in. He sees the box, and then he decides." She poured milk into a small measuring cup and thought for a moment about how to make him not see.

Lia tapped her pen against her chin. "So don't let him see."

"Right." Paisley carried the boxes behind her dad's old lawn mower, out of sight, and came back with masking tape and a marker. She labeled one row of bowls A and the other row B. Only she knew which row held the name brand, and she wrote the answer on a scrap of paper, folded it twice, and buried it under a coffee can of screws on the shelf. Gibson scooped cereal into the bowls with a serving spoon, careful to make each portion the same size, and Lia stirred a drop of milk into each one so the samples would match.

When the tasting started on Saturday, they set up the garage like a small lab. Ms. Wardak, who lived next door, came over first and tried both bowls, frowning slightly in a way that meant she was thinking hard. "B," she said. Paisley marked it down. Kids from her class filed through the doorway, one at a time, and each one tasted A, drank water, then tasted B. Nobody could tell which was which, so nobody's expectations could sway their answers, which was exactly what Paisley wanted. Gibson called it a blind test, and the phrase felt right, like the whole garage had its eyes covered.

By late afternoon Lia counted the tally marks. Eleven picked A, nine picked B. Paisley dug the folded paper out from under the coffee can, and her hands were a little unsteady as she opened it. The name brand was row B. Nine out of twenty people had chosen the expensive cereal, which was not quite half, and the store brand had actually won. She stared at the numbers while a breeze moved the paper in her fingers.

"We should run it again," Lia said, already flipping to a clean page in the notebook.

Gibson reached for the cereal boxes behind the mower. "Same bowls, new letters?"

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Laundry is sorted by colour because new dark or bright clothes can release dye into the wash water, and that dye can tint white and pale clothes.
story:
Evelyn stood in the garage in front of the washing machine with three baskets around her feet and a folded note from her mom in her hand. The note said she was in charge of her own laundry now, start to finish, and that the white school shirts had to last until June. That was the part that worried her, because Monday's white shirt had come out of the last load faintly pink, and nobody could tell her why.

She dumped the baskets out and sorted. Whites went in one pile, darks in another, and a heap of brights in a third. Then she sat cross-legged and went through the whites piece by piece, wondering what had gone wrong. The pink was even, not blotchy, which seemed strange. If something had spilled, it would have made a spot, wouldn't it? An even colour meant the pink had been everywhere in the water at once.

She dug through the laundry hamper and found it, balled up in a corner: a red sock, brand new, the tag still slightly stiff. On Monday that sock had shared a load with her white shirt. Could a sock give off colour into the water, the way a teabag gives off colour into hot water? She held the sock under the tap and watched the water run pale red. So that was it. New dark or bright clothes could release dye into the wash water, and that dye could tint white and pale clothes. She almost laughed. The sock had been a traitor hiding in the wrong pile.

Her friend Marissa came through the side door with her skateboard under her arm, looking for the helmet she had left on the workbench. "Why are you staring at a sock?" she asked.

"I figured out the pink shirt mystery. This sock leaked dye into the wash, and my white shirt soaked it up. Which is sort of ironic, since the sock was too small to matter and it ruined the biggest thing in the load." Evelyn held it up like evidence in a courtroom.

"That's a whole science happening in your garage." Marissa found her helmet and buckled it under her chin. "Don't hit your head on the dryer door, you'll get a concussion and it'll be my fault for distracting you."

Evelyn set up a test anyway, because guessing wasn't the same as knowing. She put the red sock in a small bucket of warm water with an old white pillowcase, swished it around, and waited while Marissa practiced kickflips on the driveway. After ten minutes the pillowcase had gone pink at the edges. Case closed. She added a cup of white vinegar to the bucket for the sock, made a note to wash new bright things alone from now on, and loaded the machine with pure whites only. As the drum started to turn, she measured out the detergent and said, mostly to herself, "June, here we come."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The Scottish botanist Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831 while studying orchid cells.
story:
Nolan crouched at the edge of the pond with a jar in one hand and a worksheet in the other, and both were going badly. The worksheet had three empty boxes labeled cell wall, cell membrane, and nucleus, and the jar was supposed to hold a sample of pond water for the second half of the assignment. Ms. García had set up two microscopes on the folding table by the dock, and she had been clear about the deadline: the bus back to school left at two o'clock sharp, and anyone without a finished sheet was staying behind with her to finish it Monday.

"You're on the onion first," Esme said, waving him toward the table. "I already did mine." She held up her worksheet, and Nolan's stomach dropped. Every box was filled in, and her sketch of the cells looked tidy, like a honeycomb. "I want the pond water slide," she went on. "Asees says there's a paramecium in there, and I want to see it before anyone else finds one. I've been wanting to see one move since sixth grade."

Nolan peeled a paper-thin layer from the onion half Ms. García had left on the tray, laid it on the slide, and lowered the lens. At first he saw nothing but a gray blur. He turned the focus knob a hair at a time, hesitant, because the last time he had rushed it he had cracked a slide in science class and been given the cleanup job for a week. Then the blur sharpened into rows of boxes, wall to wall, like bricks that had been told to colonize every inch of the glass. He could see the thick outer lines easily. That had to be the wall. Inside each brick was a faint rim, which he decided was the membrane.

But the third box was the problem. Somewhere in each cell there should be a dark spot, and he could not find it. He swept the slide, corner to corner, and reasoned it out loud. "The wall and membrane are outlines, so the nucleus is probably a thing floating inside, not a border. Maybe I'm in the wrong category of cell." Esme leaned over, still holding her finished sheet, drumming her fingers because the pond water was waiting for her. "It's the dark blob," she said. "Mine looked like a fingerprint in the middle of each brick. Keep looking, but be fast."

He slowed the sweep and looked for dark instead of looking for shapes. There, in cell after cell, a small dense dot, plain once he stopped expecting something bigger. He wrote nucleus in the last box just as Asees jogged up with the news that the paramecium was, in fact, swimming. "Who even found that first?" Nolan asked, still writing. "Robert Brown," Esme said, grinning. "Some Scottish botanist. He described the nucleus in 1831 looking at orchid cells. Ms. García told me when I asked who first noticed the dark spot." Asees shouted from the dock that the thing was turning left. Esme shoved her worksheet into Nolan's hand for proof of her head start and ran, and Nolan capped his pen at 1:53, following her down to the water.

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: Putting a little air in a new tube before fitting it gives it shape, so it is less likely to twist or get pinched under the tyre.
story:
Bike club met behind the gym on Thursdays, and this Thursday Payton had a problem: her back tyre was flat as a pancake, and the school's Fun Ride was in three days. Mr. Koné dumped a bucket of tyre levers, patches and a pump on the tarmac and said, "Fix it yourselves. I'm only here to convert your groaning into effort." He sat on a crate with his coffee like a king watching peasants.

The tyre levers were the easy part. Payton snapped two of them under the rim, popped the bead loose, and pulled out the old tube with a hiss of dying dignity. Brodie held the wheel steady while Charlee found the hole, spit on the tube, and watched the bubbles. "Culprit located," Charlee announced, like a detective. Then they all stared at the new tube, pale and floppy, like a noodle that had given up on life.

The hard part began when Payton tried to put the noodle back in. Every time she pushed the tyre onto the rim, the tube slithered out of place and got trapped under the bead. She levered, cursed under her breath, started again. Three times the tube bulged out at one spot like a sleepy animal trying to escape. "It's mocking me," she told the wheel.

She stopped and thought. The tube kept twisting because it had no shape, the way a rope tangles but a stick doesn't. If the tube had a shape, it might sit still. There was a pump right there. She hooked it up and put a little air in, just enough that the tube puffed into a rounded circle instead of a sad ribbon. It held its form in the tyre like it had been told to sit up straight. The tyre slid back on in one smooth push, and nothing got caught, nothing got pinched. "It needed a spine," she said, and pumped it up proper.

"Dormant genius activated," said Charlee, offering a solemn high five. Brodie wrote something in his notebook under PAYTON'S LAW, which was a factor he claimed would one day convert the whole school to her fandom.

Then Payton turned the wheel proudly and heard the thin, unmistakable whistle of air escaping from the front tyre, which had been fine all morning. Mr. Koné raised his coffee cup without getting up. "Bucket's still there," he said.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A glow stick shines brighter but runs out faster when it is warm, and glows dimmer but lasts longer when it is cold.
story:
Riley stood in front of the mirror at Trend Junction with three dresses over her arm and twenty minutes before Sami's mom arrived to drive them to the dance. The mall speakers blasted an aggressive jingle about the store's anniversary sale, and Macy held up a fourth dress, silver and short. "This one," Macy said. "It's literally made for a dance."

"Everything here is literally made for a dance," Riley said, but she took it anyway. At the register, wedged between racks of clearance scarves, a bin of glow sticks sat beside a sign: FREE WITH ANY PURCHASE, WHILE SUPPLIES LAST. Riley, who had learned in Mr. Bakker's class to be suspicious of anything free in a place of commerce, took two anyway and slipped one into her pocket.

At the dance she cracked the first stick and clipped it to her wrist, and it blazed so bright that Sami grabbed her arm to make her wave it around. Riley's pocket, though, sat right against the gym's hot radiator through the whole first hour, and when she cracked the second stick later it flared brilliantly and then, by the last song, went dark while the first one still glowed on her wrist. She turned the dead stick over in her hand, thinking. It had been warm in her pocket. The first one had lived in the cool dark of her locker all afternoon, dimmer but still alive. There was a pattern here, she thought, something you couldn't see directly, and only one way to test it.

"Come home with me," she told Macy on the bus. "I need your freezer."

"You need my freezer," Macy repeated. But she came, and Riley retrieved the first glow stick, the dim one, from her jacket and laid it in the ice tray between two cubes of frozen orange juice. "If it's still glowing in the morning, I'm right," she said. "Cold keeps it going longer."

"Why do you care?" Macy asked, flopping onto Riley's bed. "The dance is over."

Riley thought about the silver dress, still hanging in the closet with the tags on because she'd worn Sami's borrowed skirt instead at the last minute, and about the bin at the store. She had taken the free sticks without questioning them, the way she'd said yes to the dance without deciding whether she actually wanted to go. "Because next time I'll know," she said. "Bright and fast, or dim and slow. You have to pick."

In the morning they ran downstairs in their socks. Macy yanked open the freezer door and pulled back the juice cubes.

The glow stick was glowing.
